title: Stanford Study: AI Makes Developers 20% More Productive (But There's a Catch)
summary: Fractional CTO livestream reacting to the Stanford 100k-developer productivity talk.

assertions.quote: you're going to be 15 to 20% more effective using AI

verdicts.note: The Stanford 100k-developer study and other field data put average gains around 10-20%, far below 2x-10x marketing claims.

assertions.quote: it doesn't take very long for your product to quickly reduce the value that AI provides

verdicts.note: Consistent across Stanford's data, METR's mature-repo slowdown and long-context degradation results.
METR names repo size and maturity (10+ years, more than 1M lines) and complex edits as factors behind the slowdown, in contrast with greenfield RCTs that found speedups.

assertions.quote: more commits doesn't mean more better ... some of those commits are cleanup

verdicts.note: Stanford and GitClear both found increased short-term churn/rework with AI, so raw commit/PR counts inflate apparent gains.

METR warns that lines of code and task counts can rise without productivity (more verbose but equivalent code). Developers wrote 47% more code per hour with AI (not significant) while being slower. This doesn't cover the rework mechanism.

Builds rose 38% vs 26% for PRs; authors note this could reflect trial-and-error coding that lowers quality, but build success rate fell significantly only at Accenture (-17%), pooled -5.5% NS, so rework is suggested not shown.

assertions.quote: people telling you estimating how their productivity was affected by AI is effectively a coin flip

verdicts.note: METR found devs believed they were ~20% faster while measured slower; other studies also show self-reports outrunning measured gains.
Developers forecast a 24% speedup and afterward estimated 20%, but were actually slowed 19%. Experts also overestimated, predicting 38-39% faster.
In the Copilot RCT both groups estimated a ~35% productivity gain, an underestimate of the measured 55.8% speedup.

METR Feb 2026: some developers self-report very high speedups, which METR notes can be 'quite unreliable' per its earlier study; it also says the true speedup may be higher among those who selected out, so no new measured overestimate.
Anthropic's +50% figures are self-reported; the post cites METR's overestimation finding and admits perception, social-desirability and recall biases, so it cannot settle the question.

assertions.quote: It can handle more, but it quickly drops off at how effective it can be

verdicts.note: Long-context benchmarks (e.g. NoLiMa, context-rot studies) show degradation as context grows; the exact threshold is model-dependent.

assertions.quote: if you can break your work down into smaller digestible chunks, it's easier for you to do that work

verdicts.note: Small batches with fast feedback are a strong DORA predictor of delivery performance; DORA 2024 linked AI to larger batches and lower stability.
